tier_reason: The only number is a single first-party sentence, 'On high-bandwidth connections it is able to seed at 3 times the speed of the official client', from the project's old description. It comes with no methodology, hardware, versions, torrent size or peer count, so it is first-party numbers without methodology (C). It is not in the current README or the v0.13.0 README.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 'On high-bandwidth connections it is able to seed at 3 times the speed of the official client.' (old first-party project description, verbatim in the SlackBuilds 14.1 libtorrent README for libtorrent 0.13.6; no methodology)
corrections.caveats: The 3x sentence was verified verbatim in the SlackBuilds 14.1 package README (GitHub mirror SlackBuildsOrg/slackbuilds, libtorrent 0.13.6). slackbuilds.org itself is egress-blocked, and the 14.0 path does not exist in the mirror. The sentence comes from the project's old description and is in neither the current README nor the v0.13.0 README. The current README keeps only the design point ('transferring directly from file pages to the network stack') and 'high performance' with no numbers. The baseline 'official client' is vague (the original mainline BitTorrent client of that era). No methodology, hardware, torrent size, peer count or versions are given, so the claim is old, first-party and unreproducible, and it predates the heavily reworked current 0.16.x code. Off-category for event-loops-io: this is a BitTorrent engine, and the baseline is a BitTorrent client, not libuv, libevent or epoll. GPL-2.0 is copyleft.

notes: Real, active project (last commit 2026-10-06, release 0.16.25 on 2026-10-05; GPL-2.0, about 1k stars, not a fork or archived; metadata correct). The 3x claim was confirmed verbatim in a reachable SlackBuilds mirror, so benchmark_url now points there. Shortcomings: a decades-old first-party marketing sentence with no methodology, a vague baseline, and a category fit (event-loops-io) that is a stretch.

tier_reason: The README Performance table (llhttp 1777.24 mb/s, 3583799.39 req/sec, 4.61 s vs http_parser 694.66 mb/s, 1406180.33 req/sec, 11.79 s; 'approximately 156%' faster) is first-party. It states no CPU, compiler or flags. The current bench/native.ts runs llhttp only, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from the current tree: C.

corrections.workload: Repeatedly parsing a single ~518-byte chunked POST request (http_parser's bench.c fixture: 'POST /joyent/http-parser HTTP/1.1' with 11 headers and an 11-byte chunk) until 8 GiB (8192 mb) is consumed. Each run reports mb/s, req/sec and wall time. The table's bytes per request (518 for http_parser, about 520 for llhttp, derived from page data) match bench.c and llhttp's own copy of that request in bench/native.ts, which adds the final CRLF.
corrections.caveats: First-party README numbers only: no CPU, compiler or flags, and the table is undated. The http_parser row (694.66 mb/s, 1406180.33 req/sec, 11.79 s) is identical to two decimals in the v1.0.1 README and has never been re-measured. The llhttp row was raised from 1497.88 to 1777.24 mb/s at v2.0.0, whose release notes credit an llparse bump with 20-28% more speed. The headline 2.56x therefore probably pairs a newer llhttp run with an older baseline run, and same machine and session are not shown. The current bench/native.ts and bench/wasm.ts time llhttp only (the http_parser side lives in http_parser's own bench.c, which the table's output format matches), so the comparison is not reproducible from llhttp's tree. The Makefile builds the library with clang -Os -g3, so the benchmark flags are unknown. llhttp is itself a named baseline of the http-parsers category, and this record is its win over its predecessor http_parser (also a named baseline). A single hot-cache request, repeated, measures small-message parsing speed, not mixed traffic. No independent comparison was found (one WebSearch; the Node.js blog and author posts are egress-blocked).

notes: README numbers match the claim exactly (2.56x bandwidth derived from page data); metadata correct (MIT, 1.9k stars, last commit 2026-10-01, active, not a fork). Main shortcomings: first-party, no hardware or compiler, the baseline row is carried unchanged from v1.0.1 while the llhttp row was re-measured at v2.0.0, and there is no public harness in the repo for the http_parser side. llhttp is a category baseline (http-parsers), not already listed as an entry; no duplicate found.
